pr_title: Make DISTINCT ON respect the ORDER BY clause similar to Postgres + several ordered aggregate improvements
pr_body:
Fixes #2041, fixes #6061 , fixes #6524

This PR reworks the DISTINCT ON operator so that it orders values not named in the ON list. It does this by pushing the `ORDER BY` clause for any elements not in the target list into the `FIRST` aggregates that are pushed as part of the `DISTINCT ON`. 

For example, a query like this:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT ON (i) i, j FROM integers ORDER BY i, j DESC;
```

Is now translated into this:

```sql
SELECT i, FIRST(j ORDER BY j DESC) FROM integers GROUP BY i ORDER BY i, j DESC;
```

This makes our `DISTINCT ON` operator match what [Postgres' DISTINCT ON does](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html#SQL-DISTINCT).

#### Ordered Aggregates

This PR also includes a number of improvements to ordered aggregates.

* Ordered aggregates are bound during **physical planning** instead of during binding. As a result, the `ORDER BY` information is kept in the optimizer phase, and optimizers and other nodes have insight into the order modifiers of an aggregate.
* We introduce an `AggregateOrderDependent` property that determines for aggregate functions whether or not their input order matches. If an `ORDER BY` clause is used for an aggregate on which this has no effect (e.g. `min`, `max` or `median`) the `ORDER BY` clause is removed.
* We add code that removes redundant/unnecessary entries from the `ORDER BY` lists of aggregates - namely (1) we remove duplicate entries, and (2) we remove any columns that are part of the `GROUP BY` list from the `ORDER BY`. The second can be done because, **within a group**, the entries that are part of the `GROUP BY` are always constant, hence ordering by them does not change the result at all.

issue_context.title: SELECT DISTINCT ON does not return the right rows
issue_context.body:
DuckDB 0.2.7 on Windows 10

Based on [https://stackoverflow.com/a/46567397](https://stackoverflow.com/a/46567397)

The DISTINCT ON clause should be executed after the ORDER BY clause.

Sorry, I'm having trouble properly formatting the SQL from the StackOverflow page.
comments: just hit this too, workaround is to do the ordering in a subquery, note in my case the ordering column is double not int which might be relevant
Can you try to make a reproducible example following the issue template please?

I see. What makes you think the `DISTINCT ON` should be evaluated *after* the `ORDER BY`? Is this somewhere in the SQL standard? The link you sent appears to indicate Postgres does this, but the example you gave produces an error in Postgres: ` SELECT DISTINCT ON expressions must match initial ORDER BY expressions`

re: the postgres error perhaps the correct syntax is
```
select distinct on(a) a, b from foo order by a, b desc;
```
which should yield the same result... but i don't have access to a shell right now

the reasoning for the proposed evaluation order is that currently `DISTINCT ON` yields random results, which renders it useless in many real life use cases -- the SO link provides one, another common scenario is selecting the desired row for each range in a range join

also since the behavior hasn't been deterministic up until this point, enforcing this evaluation order wouldn't be breaking

from a bit of googling i can't find any other sql impl that has `DISTINCT ON`, so i'm guessing we got the inspiration from postgres and it would make sense to follow the behavior there... (documentation reproduced here https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.0/sql-select.html#SQL-DISTINCT)
@hannes checking in to see if any other info would help w/ further discussion here thanks

> What makes you think the `DISTINCT ON` should be evaluated _after_ the `ORDER BY`?

For me, the whole point of `distinct on` is syntatic sugar to filter a table for the max/min element of a group. Without `distinct on` you have to resort to joining on a subquery. The `distinct on` syntax is more concise, clearer, and IMHO more beautiful.

If `distinct on` simply returns a random value from the group it's not useful for this use-case. Maybe there other use-cases for it IDK, but by applying the `DISTINCT ON` *after* the `ORDER BY` it allows it to be used for filtering on the latest/max/min per group which makes it much more useful/powerful.

As @kevinykuo points out, the current implementation returns a random match (the first value in the set of matches) so changing it to return the first value after the `ORDER BY` clause has been applied is backward-compatible (modulo [`#1172`](https://xkcd.com/1172/))

----

Example showing that, as implemented, `DISTINCT ON` just returns the first value of a random set of matches rather than either the smallest or largest value (of `b`)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/881019/216973928-8c87933c-fa06-41db-b009-602699410bf5.png)

What you have to do without `DISTINCT ON` to get the max/min `b` per group (`a`):

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/881019/216977015-8d4fbaf9-d213-452d-898d-09a7fa4ce5be.png)

I don't quite understand why the regular `min` and `max` aggregates would not work in your example? Finding the minimum value of `b` for a group `a` is exactly what `GROUP BY` does, no?

```sql
D select a, max(b) from foo group by a;
┌───────┬────────┐
│   a   │ max(b) │
│ float │ float  │
├───────┼────────┤
│   1.0 │  420.0 │
│   2.0 │  420.0 │
└───────┴────────┘
D select a, min(b) from foo group by a;
┌───────┬────────┐
│   a   │ min(b) │
│ float │ float  │
├───────┼────────┤
│   1.0 │   53.0 │
│   2.0 │   53.0 │
└───────┴────────┘
```

Sorry, bad example. I think you can't use `max` where you want to get the value of other columns, not in the `GROUP BY`? I think it might also not work for duplicate max values (neither does the join above). e.g. ``` create table foo(a real, b real, c real); insert into foo values (1, 69, 1), (1, 53, 2), (1, 420, 3), (1, 420, 4), (2, 55, 1), (2, 69, 2), (2,53, 3), (2, 420, 4); ``` ``` with T1 as ( select * from foo order by b desc ) select distinct on(a) a, b, c from T1 ```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/881019/216998647-a3ea50a9-ba1d-4857-aff3-58f7b0668a0b.png) ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/881019/216999406-1e376ff9-8222-4bc2-9b08-990ef3ae8a9b.png)
---- ***Edit:*** Maybe that's what `ANY_VALUE` is for - I'm not familiar with that: ``` con.execute("select a, max(b), c from foo group by a;").arrow().to_pandas() ``` > `BinderException: Binder Error: column "c" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or must be part of an aggregate function. Either add it to the GROUP BY list, or use "ANY_VALUE(c)" if the exact value of "c" is not important. LINE 1: select a, max(b), c from foo group by a;`

You can use `max_by` or `min_by` for that, e.g.:

```sql
select a, max(b), max_by(c, b), min_by(c, b) from foo group by a;
┌───────┬────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐
│   a   │ max(b) │ max_by(c, b) │ min_by(c, b) │
│ float │ float  │    float     │    float     │
├───────┼────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┤
│   1.0 │  420.0 │          3.0 │          2.0 │
│   2.0 │  420.0 │          4.0 │          3.0 │
└───────┴────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘
```

As a side-note, instead of using `.arrow().to_pandas()` it should be faster to use `.df()` directly.

Thanks, that's good to know! I'm just getting started out with `duckdb` so I'm still figuring things out.

That's in fact how I ended up here - I was looking to see if `duckdb` supported postgres' `DISTINCT ON` command. I'm glad I found this issue as if I had of used it as I would have in postgres I would have gotten silently incorrect results which might have been quite tricky to track down.

All other things being equal, I thing it would be good to align with the postgres implementation, if only to prevent users familiar with that from shooting themselves in the foot.

review_comments: Being order dependent is very unusual - I think it makes developing other aggregates simpler to make that the default.

I thought about that as well, I opted for not doing so for two reasons:

* There are many aggregates that are "surprisingly" order dependent, like the floating point sum that you mentioned, or anything with floating point instabilities. In that case we might still want to allow users to add an `ORDER BY` clause. 
* It is quite tough to automatically test whether or not an aggregate is order dependent - so it is not easy to notify the developer that they have set this property incorrectly. I imagine this will lead to subtle bugs when writing new aggregates. This is essentially opting to perform the ORDER BY unless the developer is certain the aggregate is not order dependent.
Is it worth making this the default?
One thing I noticed looking at serializing sorted aggregates is that we are not set up to handle aggregate wrappers. But we may be able to deal with that now?
